title: Habitats: how plants and animals are suited to their homes
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 2 Biology, Unit 1.1 'Habitats', Unit 1.2 'Plants in different habitats' and Unit 1.3 'Animals in different habitats'. No textbook needed.
summary: A cactus would rot in a pond, and a lotus would dry up in the desert. Why? Your child learns the word habitat and meets ponds, deserts, forests, seashores and snowy mountains. They find out how each body solves a problem of its home: a cactus stem stores water, water rolls off a lotus leaf, a fish has gills, a camel has wide feet. They build a sealed bottle garden that makes its own rain, look for signs of hidden animals, and argue about whether a zoo can be a real habitat.
builds_on: Class 1: every place is somebody's home. Living things live where they find food, water and shelter. Mould grew only on damp bread, and seedlings in the dark grew pale. Next: Class 3 looks at how plants and animals share one tree and its soil. Class 4 studies India's deserts, mountains, plains and coasts and how people live there. Class 5 learns the word adaptation fully, endemic species, and predators and prey.
goals: By the end your child can say what a habitat is and name five different habitats.
By the end your child can explain how a cactus, a lotus and a pine tree are each suited to where they grow.
By the end your child can explain how a fish, a camel and a polar bear are each suited to where they live.
By the end your child can find and read signs that an animal lives nearby (tracks, droppings, nests, holes, chewed leaves).
By the end your child can describe how water keeps going round inside a sealed bottle garden.
By the end your child can give one reason for and one against keeping wild animals in zoos.
words: habitat
the natural home of a plant or animal, which gives them food, water, shelter, space and the right temperature
microhabitat
a very small habitat inside a bigger one, like the underside of a leaf or the inside of a log
suited
having a body that fits their home well (scientists say adapted)
desert
a place that gets very little rain. It can be hot or cold.
pond
a small area of still water
gills
the parts of a fish that take oxygen out of water
waxy
covered with a smooth, shiny coat that water runs off
spines
the sharp points on a cactus. They are the cactus's leaves, changed in shape.
evidence
something you can see or find that shows something is true
condensation
water in the air turning back into drops on a cool surface
subconcepts: a habitat gives food, water, shelter, space and the right temperature
comparing habitats: pond, forest, desert, seashore, grassland, snowy mountain
plants in dry places: cactus stems store water, spines are leaves
plants in wet places: floating lotus and waxy leaves
plants in cold places: pine needles and sloping branches
animals in water: gills, fins and webbed feet
animals in deserts and snow: camel, polar bear, snow leopard
suited to a home: the beginning of the idea of adaptation
animal signs: tracks, droppings, nests, holes and nibbles
a sealed bottle garden: water going round and round
people change habitats, for harm and for care
plants change with height up a mountain

days.title: Every home is a habitat
days.goal: Recall last year's homes and learn what a habitat must give.

steps.title: Remember Class 1
steps.do: Ask: 'Last year we found who lives in our house. Where did the mould grow? Who lived under the pot?' (Mould on the damp bread, ants or woodlice under the pot, because it was dark, damp and safe.) Say: 'Scientists have a word for a living thing's natural home. It is habitat.' Say it together, clapping the three beats: ha-bi-tat.

steps.title: Five things a habitat gives
steps.do: Hold up one hand and name one thing per finger: food, water, shelter, space, the right temperature. For each, ask your child to think of an animal who would be in trouble without it: a fish with no water, a tiger with no space to hunt, a polar bear in the Chennai heat. Then ask: 'Is our home a habitat for us? Which of the five does it give us?'

steps.title: Habitat sort
steps.do: Do Activity a1. Draw six big circles on paper and label them: pond, forest, desert, seashore, grassland, snowy mountain. Your child draws living things, or cuts pictures from old magazines, and puts each one in their habitat: frog and lotus (pond), tiger and hornbill (forest), camel and cactus (desert), crab and coconut palm (seashore), blackbuck and grass (grassland), snow leopard and pine (snowy mountain). For each one ask: 'What does this habitat give them?' Some can go in two places. Let your child argue it.

steps.title: A habitat inside a habitat
steps.do: Hold a leaf from a potted plant. Say: 'A forest is a big habitat. But the underside of one leaf is a tiny habitat too, for an aphid or a small spider. A tiny habitat inside a big one is called a microhabitat.' Ask: 'Can you find a microhabitat in this room?' (a crack in the wall, the soil in a pot, the corner of the window).

steps.title: Say it back
steps.do: Your child finishes: 'A habitat is…' (the natural home of a living thing, which gives them food, water, shelter, space and the right temperature).

need: a leaf from a potted plant

days.title: A habitat in a bottle
days.goal: Build a sealed bottle garden and hear how glass boxes once carried habitats across the sea.

steps.title: Build the bottle garden
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Build the sealed bottle garden together. Your child chooses where to put each plant and waters lightly, and you close the lid. Ask: 'If we never open it and never water it again, will the plants live or die? Why do you think so?' Write down the answer. Put the bottle in bright light but not direct sun.

steps.title: Story: The Glass Garden
steps.do: Read the story 'The Glass Garden' aloud. A boy carries tea plants on a ship from China to India. Don't explain it. Ask the story questions, especially: 'Why did the seedlings in the glass boxes live, when the ones in baskets died?'

steps.title: Dr Ward's accident
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v1. Nathaniel Ward, a doctor in London, could not grow ferns in his smoky garden. One day he found a tiny fern growing by itself inside a sealed glass bottle, where he had put a moth's cocoon in damp soil. The bottle kept its own clean, damp air. Ask the voice question. Then look at your own bottle: is there any mist on the glass yet?

steps.title: Dance the bottle's rain
steps.do: Dance the water inside the bottle garden. Your child starts curled on the floor as a drop of water in the soil. They rise slowly on tiptoe, arms floating up: the water evaporates into the air. They touch the 'cold glass' (a wall) and freeze: the water condenses into a drop. They slide slowly down the wall to the floor: the drop runs back to the soil. Do it three times. Ask: 'Did the water go away, or did it come back?'

need: a big clean transparent bottle or jar with a lid
a handful of charcoal pieces, if you have them
soil from a pot, or a small bag of potting soil from a nursery
2 or 3 small plants that like shade and damp, such as money plant cuttings or small ferns from a nursery
a spoon and a long stick

days.title: Plants in dry places and wet places
days.goal: Find out how a cactus and a lotus each fit their habitat.

steps.title: Check the bottle
steps.do: Look at the bottle garden. Is there mist or drops on the inside of the glass? Ask: 'Where did they come from?' Then explain: water from the soil and the leaves went into the air, and turned back into drops on the cool glass. This is called condensation. The drops run back down, so the bottle makes its own rain.

steps.title: The leaf that water can't wet
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Drip water on a colocasia leaf (chembu or arbi), a cabbage leaf and a sheet of paper. Watch the drops. Your child rolls a drop around the leaf like a marble. Ask: 'A lotus lives in a pond, with leaves lying on the water. Why would it help the lotus if water rolls off the leaf?' (The leaf stays clean and dry, and its tiny breathing holes, which are on the top of the leaf, stay open to the air.)

steps.title: The cactus and the sponge
steps.do: First the problem: a cactus lives where it rains very little, so she must not lose the water she has. Wet two equal sponges or folded cloths. Wrap one in a plastic bag with one small hole, and leave the other open. Put both in the sun. Ask: 'Which will stay wet longer?' Check at the end of the day. Then look at an aloe vera or a cactus in a pot, carefully, or a picture. The fat stem is full of water and has a waxy skin. Instead of leaves it has spines. Big flat leaves lose water into the air. Spines lose almost none, and they stop thirsty animals biting the water-filled stem. Ask: 'Which sponge is like a cactus?'

steps.title: Humboldt climbs a mountain
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v2. In 1802, Alexander von Humboldt and the plant scientist Aimé Bonpland climbed a huge mountain in South America. They wrote down the plants at each height. Near the bottom there was hot forest. Higher up, grass and bushes. Near the snow, only tiny tough plants and lichens. Ask: 'Why would different plants live at the top and the bottom of one mountain?' (It is colder higher up.) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Two plants, two homes
steps.do: Ask: 'Could a cactus live in a pond? Could a lotus live in the desert? Why not?' Listen for: the cactus's roots would rot in the water, and the lotus would dry up because she cannot store water.

need: a colocasia (chembu or arbi) leaf, or a lotus leaf
2 sponges or cloths and a plastic bag
an aloe vera or cactus in a pot, or a picture of one

days.title: Plants in cold places, and plants near us
days.goal: See how cold-country trees fit their habitat, and find where plants can and cannot grow near home.

steps.title: Snow on a roof
steps.do: Hold a flat plate next to a cone made of paper. Sprinkle rice or salt on both, as 'snow'. Ask: 'Which one holds the snow? Which one lets it slide off?' Show a picture of a pine or deodar tree. Pines grow in Kashmir and Shimla, and there is a pine forest at Kodaikanal. Their branches slope down like a cone, and their leaves are thin needles. Ask: 'How would that help in snow?' (Heavy snow slides off instead of breaking the branches. Thin, waxy needles lose little water when the ground is frozen and roots cannot drink.)

steps.title: Where can plants grow?
steps.do: Walk around your building or street with Worksheet ws1, Section A. Find plants in surprising places: in a crack in the pavement, on top of a wall, on a terrace, near a drain, on a tree's bark (moss, ferns, peepal seedlings). Also find places with NO plants: under a parked car, on a busy path, in a dark stairwell. At each, ask: 'What is missing here: light, water, soil, or peace from feet?' Your child writes or draws a few in the worksheet.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Finish Worksheet ws1, Sections B and C. Read the questions aloud. For the 'why' questions, your child says the answer and you write it in their words.

steps.title: The peepal on the wall
steps.do: Ask: 'A peepal seedling is growing on top of a wall. How did the seed get up there?' (A bird ate a peepal fig and left the seed in their droppings.) 'Do you think the peepal will grow big? What does she need that the wall can't give?'

need: a handful of rice or salt
a picture of a pine or deodar tree

days.title: Animals made for their homes
days.goal: Notice how animals' bodies fit their habitats, and design one.

steps.title: Check the bottle
steps.do: Look at the bottle garden again. Is it still misty? Are the plants alive? Ask: 'We haven't watered it for days. Where is their water coming from?' (The same water goes round: soil, plant, air, glass, soil.)

steps.title: Body parts and habitats
steps.do: Use pictures or a phone. Go through five animals. For each, first say the problem, then point at the body part and ask: 'How does this help them?' Fish: they must get air from water. Gills take oxygen out of the water. Duck: they swim on ponds. Webbed feet push water like paddles, and oiled feathers stay dry. Camel: they walk on soft sand with little food. Wide padded feet don't sink, long eyelashes and nostrils that close keep sand out, and the hump is fat, stored food (not water). Polar bear: they live on ice. Thick fur and a layer of fat keep them warm, and white fur hides them on snow. Frog: they live in water and on land. They have lungs, and also breathe through their wet skin. Ask: 'Which of these animals would be in trouble in another one's home?'

steps.title: Design a creature
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Your child picks one habitat (pond, desert, snowy mountain, seashore or forest) and invents a new animal who would live there well. They draw the animal and label three body parts with what each one is for. Ask: 'Where does your animal find water? How do they stay warm, or cool? Where do they hide?' A good design gives a reason for every part.

steps.title: Swap the homes
steps.do: Ask: 'Could your animal live in a different habitat? What would go wrong?' Then do two yoga poses named after animals: camel pose (ustrasana: kneel, hands on heels, chest up) and fish pose (matsyasana: lie back with the chest lifted). Breathe three times in each. Say the word scientists use: an animal is adapted to their habitat when their body and way of living fit it.

need: pictures of a fish, duck, camel, polar bear and frog (books or phone)

days.title: Hidden homes and animal signs
days.goal: Find evidence of animals we cannot see, and think about zoos.

steps.title: Animal clue hunt
steps.do: Say: 'Animals often hide. We will be detectives and find evidence that they are here.' Look around your building: the stairs, the terrace, the parking area, the balcony pots. If you have a park or garden nearby, go there too. Look for: footprints in dust or mud (birds, dogs, cats), holes in the ground (rats, ants), droppings, feathers, spider webs, nests, leaves with holes or wiggly tunnels (caterpillars), silvery slime trails (snails). For each clue, your child draws it and guesses who left it. Ask: 'How sure are you? What other clue would make you more sure?'

steps.title: Is a zoo a habitat?
steps.do: Talk about voice v3. Ask first: 'Have you been to a zoo? Did the animals look happy?' Then give the evidence on both sides. Zoos have saved some animals from dying out and help people care about wild animals. But many big animals, like elephants, live much shorter lives in zoos than in the wild, and some walk up and down the same path over and over. Ask the voice question. Let your child decide and give a reason.

steps.title: Best clue
steps.do: Your child picks the best clue of the day and explains to someone in the family who left it and how they know. Check the bottle garden on the way home.

need: a magnifying glass, if you have one

days.title: Caring for habitats, and teach it back
days.goal: Think about how people change habitats, play the game and teach it back.

steps.title: Harm and care
steps.do: Ask: 'What happens to a pond if someone throws plastic in it? To a forest if it is cut for a road?' Then ask: 'What can people do to make a habitat better?' Good answers: plant trees, leave a corner wild, put out water bowls for birds in summer, clean a pond, keep beach lights off at night so baby turtles find the sea. Look at your bottle garden: 'What would happen if we left it in hot sun? If we opened it and dropped in a sweet wrapper?'

steps.title: Habitat Hop board game
steps.do: Play the board game g1. When a player lands on a habitat square, they must name one plant or animal that lives there and one body part that helps them.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2 together. Read each item aloud and let your child answer before you write. If your child enjoys it, do Worksheet ws3 another day.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child shows the bottle garden and the animal design to the family and explains: what a habitat gives, how a cactus and a lotus fit their homes, how a camel or a fish fits their home, and how the bottle makes its own rain. Then ask the check questions. If your child enjoys thinking hard, do Worksheet ws3.

need: the printed board, a die and counters

sections.p: Write three places you found plants, and one place you found none.
A peepal seedling is growing on top of a wall. How did the seed probably get there?
opts: the wind blew a peepal tree up there

sections.p: Match each plant to their habitat.
A cactus has spines instead of big flat leaves because…
opts: spines help the cactus grow taller

sections.p: Water runs off a lotus leaf because the leaf is…
The natural home of a plant or animal is called their ____.
Which habitat does each animal live in?
Why can't a fish live on land? Use the word gills.
Why does a camel have wide, flat feet?
A bird has long thin legs and a long sharp beak. Where does this bird probably live?
opts: at the edge of a pond, catching fish
in a hot sandy desert far from water

sections.p: What is in a camel's hump?
Where would a white fox be best hidden?
Match the body part to its job.
pairs: saving water and keeping animals off

sections.p: Water drops on the inside of the cool glass are called ____.
Our sealed bottle garden doesn't need watering because…
opts: the same water goes round and round inside
the glass makes water from nothing

sections.p: What would happen to the bottle garden in a dark cupboard? Why?
Who left this clue?
pairs: a leaf with a wiggly tunnel inside
a grey feather on the terrace

sections.p: You find a hole in the ground. How could you find out who lives in it, without digging it up?
Ladakh, in the far north of India, is very cold and gets very little rain. What is Ladakh?
opts: not a desert, because it is cold

sections.p: You climb a tall mountain. As you go higher, what plants do you usually find?
Is it a big habitat or a microhabitat?
Where is a frog suited to live?
When an animal's body fits their home well, scientists say the animal is ____ to their habitat.
Some people say zoos protect animals. Others say a cage is never a habitat. What do you think? Give one reason on each side, then your own view.
In the story 'The Glass Garden', tea seedlings lived on a long sea journey because their glass box kept their habitat with them. What would you need to take with you to live on the Moon?
People live in deserts, in snow and by the sea, but they don't have fur or gills. How do people manage?

experiments.title: A habitat in a bottle
experiments.question: Can plants live in a sealed bottle without being watered?
need: a big transparent bottle or jar with a lid (a 5-litre water bottle that a grown-up cuts and tapes, or a big jar)
charcoal pieces, if you have them
soil from a pot, or potting soil from a nursery
2 or 3 small plants that like shade: money plant cuttings or small ferns from a nursery
a spoon and a long stick
steps: Put a layer of pebbles at the bottom, so extra water can drain. Add a little charcoal if you have it, which keeps the soil fresh. Then add a thick layer of damp soil.
Make holes with the stick and plant the plants. Press the soil around them.
Spray or spoon in a little water: damp, not muddy.
Close the lid tightly.
Put it in bright light but not direct sun.
Look at it every day for two weeks. Draw it on day 1, day 3, day 7 and day 14.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'If we never water it again, will the plants live? Why do you think so?'
experiments.observe: Mist and drops form on the inside of the glass, usually in the morning, and run back down. The plants stay green. If it gets too wet and mouldy, open the lid for a day. If it dries out, add a spoon of water.
experiments.why: Water from the soil and the leaves goes into the air as invisible water vapour. When it touches the cooler glass, it turns back into drops (condensation). The drops run down into the soil, and the roots drink the water again. The same water goes round and round, like a tiny version of rain on Earth. In light, the plants also take in carbon dioxide from the air inside and give out oxygen. The bottle holds a whole small habitat: light comes from outside, and water, air and soil are inside. One bottle garden in England, planted by David Latimer in 1960, was opened only once, in 1972, to add water, and kept growing for decades.
experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts any plastic bottle. Wash hands after handling soil.

experiments.title: The leaf that water can't wet
experiments.question: Why do drops roll off some leaves?
need: a colocasia (chembu or arbi) leaf, or a lotus leaf
a dropper or spoon of water
steps: Lay the three things side by side.
Drop a few drops of water on each.
Watch the shape of the drops. Tilt each one slowly.
Sprinkle a little chalk powder on the colocasia or lotus leaf, then drip water and roll a drop across it.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will the water do on each one?'
experiments.observe: On the colocasia or lotus leaf, the drop sits up like a silver ball and rolls off, picking up the chalk as it goes. On paper the water soaks in. On cabbage the drop may sit or spread a little.
experiments.why: The lotus leaf and the colocasia leaf are covered with tiny bumps topped with wax. Water cannot spread out on them, so it forms balls that roll off and carry dirt away. Scientists call this the lotus effect, and engineers copy it to make paints and cloth that clean themselves. For a plant in a pond, it keeps the leaf clean and dry, and keeps the breathing holes on the top of the leaf open to the air.
experiments.safety: No danger. Wipe up spilled water so nobody slips.

activities.title: Habitat sort
steps: Draw six big circles: pond, forest, desert, seashore, grassland, snowy mountain.
Draw or cut out at least 12 living things.
Put each one in their habitat and say what the habitat gives them.
Put any living thing that fits two habitats on the line between them and explain why.
activities.outcome: A habitat poster with at least 12 living things, each with a reason.

activities.title: Design a creature for a habitat
steps: Choose a habitat: pond, desert, snowy mountain, seashore or forest.
Think: what is hard about living there? (too hot, too cold, no water, waves, hungry hunters)
Invent an animal whose body solves those problems.
Draw the animal and label three body parts with what each is for.
Give the animal a name and say what they eat and where they shelter.
activities.outcome: An invented animal with three labelled body parts, each explained by their habitat.

project.title: Our bottle garden diary
steps: Build the sealed bottle garden on Day 2.
Draw it on day 1, day 3, day 7 and day 14.
Each time, note: Is there mist? Are the plants green? Any new leaves? Any mould?
On Day 7, explain to the family how the water goes round inside.
Keep looking for a month and decide: is it a habitat?
project.outcome: A two-week drawn diary of a tiny sealed habitat, and an explanation of how its water goes round.

game.title: Habitat Hop
rules: Put all counters on START. Take turns to roll the die and move.
On a habitat square (POND, DESERT, FOREST, SEASHORE, SNOW, GRASSLAND), name one living thing who lives there and one body part that helps them. If you are right, move 1 extra square.
On a trouble square, follow what it says.
On a care square, move forward as it says.
squares: A fish jumps out of the water: back 2
Someone cut the forest for a road: back 3
A polar bear in the hot sun: miss a turn
You put a pot back where you found it: forward 1
You put out a water bowl for birds: forward 2

big: Is a zoo a habitat? Is a fish tank? Is a city?
If you could carry a tiny piece of your habitat with you, like the tea seedlings in their glass box, what would you take?
Humans live in deserts, snow and jungles. Are we suited to every habitat, or do we bring our habitat with us?
Who should decide what happens to a pond or a forest: the people who live near it, the government, or the animals who live in it?

challenge.q: Many people think a camel's hump is full of water. Is it?
challenge.hint: No. The hump is mostly fat, which is stored food for hard times. Camels can go a long time without water because their bodies lose very little: their droppings are very dry, they sweat little, and they let their body get hotter during the day. Why do you think the 'water hump' story is so popular?

challenge.q: People often say deserts are hot and sandy. Are all deserts hot?
challenge.hint: A desert is a place with very little rain, not a hot place. Ladakh in India, the Gobi in Mongolia and Antarctica are cold deserts. Antarctica is the biggest desert in the world. So what makes a desert hard to live in? In 1983, Aditi Pant, a sea scientist from Pune, and Sudipta Sengupta, a rock scientist, became the first Indian women to work in Antarctica, on India's third expedition there.

perspectives.who: A camel herder of the Raika (Rebari) community in Rajasthan
perspectives.view: Raika families have kept camels in the Thar desert for many generations. They know which desert plants each camel needs and where the hidden water is. Ask: who knows more about the desert habitat, a scientist who visits for a month or a family who has lived there for hundreds of years? What could each learn from the other?

perspectives.who: A fish in a fish tank
perspectives.view: The fish has water, food and a little plastic plant. The fish does not have a river, rain, a muddy bottom, other kinds of fish or space to swim far. Ask: what is missing from this habitat? Does the fish know?

Winters in Leh are far below freezing and rain is rare. Yet barley, apricots and yaks do well there, and houses are built with thick walls and flat roofs for drying food. Ask: is a cold, dry place a hard habitat, or just a different one?

perspectives.who: A sea turtle on a Chennai beach, and a fish in a dark cave
perspectives.view: Olive ridley turtles live in the sea but come onto beaches, such as those near Chennai, to lay their eggs. Some fish that live in dark caves have no working eyes. Over many generations, their family lost them. Ask: is a body that fits one home 'better', or only better for that home?

voices.idea: Ward was a London doctor who could not grow ferns in his garden because of the city's smoke. Around 1829 he noticed a fern and some grass sprouting in a sealed glass bottle where he had put a moth chrysalis in damp soil. The plants lived inside for years without new water. He designed sealed glass cases, called Wardian cases, and showed that plants could survive long sea journeys inside them.
voices.then: Plant collectors quickly took up the cases, and plants that used to die on ships now arrived alive. The cases carried tea from China to India, rubber from South America to Asia, and many other plants around the world. Often this made money for empires rather than for the people whose plants they were.
voices.now: His discovery is accepted: a sealed case keeps its water going round and keeps its air moist. The bottle gardens people keep today come from his idea.
voices.ask: Ward found his discovery by accident, because he noticed something odd in a bottle. What would you need to do to notice an accident like that?

voices.who: Alexander von Humboldt (1769–1859), Germany, and Aimé Bonpland (1773–1858), France
voices.idea: In 1802, travelling in South America, Humboldt and the plant scientist Bonpland climbed high up the volcano Chimborazo with local guides. They noted that plants change in bands as you go up: hot forest at the bottom, then cooler forest, then grassland, then only mosses and lichens near the snow. Humboldt drew a famous picture showing which plants live at which height. He saw that climbing a mountain is like travelling towards the cold poles.
voices.then: His books made him famous across Europe. Bonpland, who did much of the plant collecting and describing, became much less famous. The local guides and Indigenous people who knew the mountains were hardly named at all.
voices.now: Scientists accept that plants and animals live in zones set by temperature and rain. Today they are watching many mountain plants move higher up as the climate warms.
voices.ask: If plants are moving up mountains as the Earth warms, what happens to the plants that already live at the very top?

voices.who: Zoo scientists and their critics today
voices.idea: Supporters say good zoos breed animals who are dying out in the wild, and have helped return some, like the Arabian oryx, to the wild. They say zoos help people, especially children, care about wild animals.
voices.then: Critics point to research such as a 2008 study by Ros Clubb and others. It found that elephants in European zoos lived much shorter lives than elephants in a national park in Kenya or working elephants in Myanmar. Many big animals who roam far in the wild pace up and down in enclosures, a sign of stress.
voices.now: Scientists agree that some animals do well in zoos and some do badly, and that big, clever animals who roam far, like elephants, suffer most. Whether zoos should exist, and for which animals, is still argued.
voices.ask: How could you tell if an animal in a zoo is well, when the animal cannot tell you?

story.title: The Glass Garden
text: The ship rolled, and Ah-Lin rolled with it, and the twelve glass boxes on the deck creaked against their ropes.

He was ten years old that spring, and he had never seen the sea before. At home in the hills of Fujian, the world was green and steep and wet. Every morning a white mist climbed up out of the valleys and wrapped the tea bushes like a shawl. His father and his uncles knew everything about those bushes: when to pick the two leaves and a bud, how long to wither them, how hot the iron pan should be, how to roll the leaves with the heel of the hand until they twisted into dark threads. Ah-Lin was only learning. But he could already smell when tea was ready.

Now his father and uncles had been paid to sail with an Englishman to a country called India, to teach people there how to grow tea and make it. The Englishman's name was on the papers. The tea plants were in the boxes. Ah-Lin had come because his father would not leave him behind.

There were two kinds of boxes on deck. Some were ordinary wooden crates with sacks and baskets of seedlings packed in damp soil. And some were strange: wooden boxes with sloping glass roofs, sealed tight with putty, so that the seedlings inside looked like tiny trees living in a little glass house. The Englishman called them Wardian cases, after the doctor who invented them. The sailors called them coffins.
"They will drown in their own air," said the cook, laughing. "Plants need wind. Plants need watering."
Ah-Lin was given a job: every morning, water the seedlings in the baskets. Do not touch the glass boxes. Do not open them. Not even once.

The first week, the sea was kind. The second week, a hard wind blew from the north, cold and full of salt. It whipped across the deck and spat white spray over everything. Ah-Lin watered the baskets each morning, and each morning the little leaves looked thinner. The wind dried them as fast as he wet them. The salt sat on them in a white crust. By the third week, the seedlings in the baskets were brown and curled like burnt paper. He picked one up and it crumbled.
He sat down beside the glass boxes, very sad, and put his hands on his knees.
Inside the glass, it was misty.

He pressed his face close. The inside of the glass roof was covered in tiny drops of water, as fine as the hairs on a peach. As he watched, two drops joined, and grew heavy, and slid slowly down the slope of the glass, and fell onto the soil beside a seedling's stem.
Rain. It was raining inside the box.

The seedlings in there were green. Not just alive: green, shining, with a new pale leaf unfolding at the top of the tallest one, as soft as a cat's ear. Outside, the salt wind howled. Inside, there was no wind at all. Inside, it was still and damp and warm, and every morning the mist came up off the soil and wrapped the little bushes, and every afternoon it ran back down the glass.
Ah-Lin sat there for a long time, with the cold wind on his back, looking into the box.

It was the hills. That was what it was. Someone had put a small piece of the hills of Fujian into a glass box: the mist, the stillness, the soft wet soil, the water going up and coming down. The plants in the baskets had been taken away from their home. The plants in the glass had brought their home with them.
When his father came up on deck, Ah-Lin took his hand and showed him, without a word. His father looked for a long time too. Then he nodded slowly, the way he nodded when tea was ready.

Weeks later, the ship came up a wide brown river to a city of noise and heat, and then they travelled for many days to the north, up into mountains. The Englishman was disappointed with the first places he was shown. Too hot, said Ah-Lin's father. Too flat. Too dry. Then, one morning, they came to a steep green slope where a white mist was climbing up out of the valley, and Ah-Lin's father stopped, and breathed in, and smiled.
They opened the glass boxes there. The seedlings went into the ground on a cool grey morning, with the mist around their shoulders. They did not seem to notice that they had crossed an ocean.

Many years later, people would drink tea from those hills all over the world, and the papers would say that an Englishman had brought tea to India. Ah-Lin was an old man by then. He knew whose hands had rolled the first leaves. But mostly, when he thought of that journey, he thought of the drop of water sliding down the glass, and the little green leaf, and the moment he understood why the seedlings had lived. The glass had kept the mist, the still air and the wet soil of home around them.
story.epiphany: A habitat is the conditions a living thing needs: moisture, still air, the right temperature, soil and light. The seedlings in open baskets died because the salt wind took those away. The ones in sealed glass cases lived because the case kept those conditions, with water going round inside (condensation). The turn is Ah-Lin seeing the 'rain' inside the glass. The story is fiction built on real events: in 1851 the plant collector Robert Fortune shipped tea plants from China to India in Wardian cases, with Chinese tea workers whose skill helped start Indian tea but who are rarely named.
ask: Why did the seedlings in the baskets die?
What did Ah-Lin see inside the glass box? Where did the 'rain' come from?
What did Ah-Lin mean when he thought the plants in the glass 'had brought their home with them'?
Why did his father smile at the misty green slope?
Who do the papers say brought tea to India? Who else should be remembered?

ideas.idea: A habitat is everything a place gives a living thing.
ideas.more: Water, air, warmth, shelter, food, light and space together. The bottle garden shows that if you can keep these together, a habitat can travel.

Each body solves a problem of its home. A cactus must save water, so her stem stores it. A fish must breathe in water, so they have gills. A camel walks on soft sand, so they have wide feet. Scientists call this being adapted.

ideas.idea: The same water goes round and round.
ideas.more: In the bottle and on the whole Earth, water rises as vapour, turns to drops and falls again. The same water has been in clouds, seas, plants and animals many times.

unknowns: As the Earth warms, plants and animals are moving up mountains and towards the poles. Nobody knows which ones will manage to move in time, and what will happen to those already at the top.
How long can a sealed bottle garden survive? One has lived more than 60 years, and nobody knows the limit.
Can a zoo ever give a big animal who roams far, like an elephant, everything their habitat gives? Scientists still argue.

books.title: Over and Under the Pond
books.author: Kate Messner
books.why: A mother and child paddle across a pond while, under the water, fish, beavers and plants live their lives. Shows one habitat and its many microhabitats.

books.title: Over and Under the Snow
books.author: Kate Messner
books.why: Above the snow a girl skis. Below it, small animals stay warm in hidden tunnels. A gentle way into cold habitats.

books.title: Desert Giant: The World of the Saguaro Cactus
books.author: Barbara Bash
books.why: The life of one huge cactus and all the animals who depend on her, beautifully drawn.

books.title: Island: A Story of the Galápagos
books.author: Jason Chin
books.why: An island rises from the sea, and plants and animals arrive and change to fit it. A first look at how living things become suited to a place.

check.q: What is a habitat? What five things does it give?
check.a: The natural home of a plant or animal. Food, water, shelter, space and the right temperature.

check.q: How is a cactus suited to the desert?
check.a: Her thick stem stores water. Her waxy skin and spines (changed leaves) lose very little water, and the spines keep thirsty animals away.

check.q: How is a lotus suited to a pond?
check.a: Her big leaves lie on the water and are waxy, so water rolls off and the breathing holes on top stay open. Her roots grow in the mud at the bottom.

check.q: Name an animal and one body part that helps them in their habitat.
check.a: For example: a fish has gills to breathe underwater. A camel has wide feet for sand. A polar bear has thick fur and fat for the cold. A duck has webbed feet for paddling.

check.q: Why doesn't our bottle garden need watering?
check.a: The water goes round inside: from soil and leaves into the air, turning back into drops on the glass (condensation), and back to the soil.

check.q: What is a microhabitat? Give an example.
check.a: A tiny habitat inside a bigger one: under a leaf, inside a log, a crack in a wall.

check.q: Give one reason for and one against zoos.
check.a: For: they breed and protect animals dying out in the wild, and help people care. Against: many big animals, like elephants, live shorter, stressed lives in enclosures.
